[[画像:三田・高売布神社本殿.JPG|thumb|160px|Honden (Important Cultural Property)]]
'''Takamefu Shrine''' (たかめふじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Sanda, Hyōgo|Q847607|qid=Q847607}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290}}. It is the only {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=shikinaisha small shrine}} in Sanda City, and its former {{ill|Shakaku|Q10444029|qid=Q10444029}} was {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}} of former {{ill|Kawabe District, Hyōgo|Q1042053|qid=Q1042053}}.
The honden and wooden {{ill|Komainu|Q20155846|qid=Q20155846}} are designated national {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}}.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The main deity is {{ill|Shitateruhime|Q11307233|qid=Q11307233|lt=Shitateruhime-no-Mikoto}} (Takahime-no-Kami), with {{ill|Ame no Wakahiko|Q10940674|qid=Q10940674|lt=Ame-no-Wakahiko-no-Mikoto}} as associated deity.

=== History ===
It is traditionally said to have been founded in the time of {{ill|Empress Suiko|Q298057|qid=Q298057}}. There is also a theory relating it to the founding of {{ill|Mefu Shrine (Takarazuka)|Q3304192|qid=Q3304192|lt=Mefu Shrine}}, another shikinaisha in the same Kawabe District. In the Heian period, {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|ast|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|es|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|fa|میناموتو نو میتسوناکا|fr|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|it|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|ja|源満仲|ko|미나모토노 미쓰나카|oc|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|pt|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|sv|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|zh|源滿仲|qid=Q2531241}}, who held vast estates in the region, is said to have made it the district sōsha. There is a tradition that Mitsunaka planted a {{ill|Zelkova serrata|Q920344|qid=Q920344}} tree.

In {{ill|1626|Q6831|qid=Q6831}} ({{ill|Kan'ei|Q1192913|qid=Q1192913}} 3), it became a hereditary prayer place for the Aoki clan, lords of Asada Domain. In {{ill|1736|Q6989|qid=Q6989}} ({{ill|Genbun|Q1145754|qid=Q1145754}} 1), through research by {{ill|Namikawa Seisho|Q6563872|qid=Q6563872}} (ordered to compile local geography by temple-and-shrine magistrate {{ill|Ōoka Tadasuke|Q1054143|qid=Q1054143}}), this shrine was identified as the shikinaisha Takamefu Shrine, and thereafter came to be called Takamefu Shrine.

In {{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}} (Meiji 6) it was ranked gōsha; at the end of Meiji it integrated and merged shrines from Sakai, Tokura, Tanaka, Kawahara, Nunogi, and Sueyoshi villages, forming the present shrine.

At some period it was also called Kazuki Daimyōjin, Tsuki-no-miya, and Sai-no-miya. A shrine-name plaque reading “Senior First Rank Kazuki Daimyōjin,” donated from {{ill|Hōkyō-ji Temple|Q11452697|qid=Q11452697}} in Kyoto, remains in the haiden.

=== Shrine buildings and precincts ===
*Honden: Ichiken-sha {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}}, {{ill|cypress bark roof|ja|檜皮葺|zh|檜皮葺|qid=Q90373477}}; original construction date unknown. A ridge tag indicates rebuilding in {{ill|1513|Q6200|qid=Q6200}} ({{ill|Eishō (Muromachi period)|Q1193577|qid=Q1193577}} 10).
*Wooden komainu: carved from single blocks of {{ill|Torreya nucifera|Q1373999|qid=Q1373999}}, with inscription dated {{ill|1297|Q5562|qid=Q5562}} (Einin 5).
*Subsidiary shrines: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|Q1129330|qid=Q1129330|lt=Ebisu}} Shrine and {{ill|Inari Ōkami|Q719665|qid=Q719665|lt=Inari}} Shrine.

=== Rituals and annual events ===
*Senbon-tsuki: on October 7, fathers called "hatsutō" (whose children were born in the past year) sing "Sosoba-tsuki-uta" while making "chigiri-mikyo," rice cakes offered at the annual festival.
*Annual festival: on October 9, "chigiri-mikyo" is offered before the deity, and "hatsutō" carry the {{ill|Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940}}.
